candidates.title: MorningBlues Record R1 Makes Holiday Gifting Personal for Music Lovers
candidates.full_text:
Choosing a Christmas gift for a music lover gets more interesting when you think about the songs that mean something to them. The MorningBlues Record R1 speaker gives those favorites a place in the home, pairing a record-inspired body with album artwork and animated lyrics. It’s a gift that invites a shared listen, starting with the track you both remember for completely different reasons.

The circular body recalls a vinyl record, with the screen sitting where you’d expect the label. Solid walnut legs and acoustic fabric give it a furniture-like character, a thoughtful detail when you’re choosing something for a person who’s particular about their surroundings. There’s no spinning platter here, of course, but someone who grew up admiring record sleeves might appreciate the reference before the music even starts.

Holiday gatherings offer another reason to give the screen some attention. The R1’s nine dynamic lyric scenes put the words where people sharing the room can follow along, adding something to an after-dinner playlist beyond background music. An old favorite could turn into an impromptu sing-along, or finally settle an argument about a misheard line. Of course, some relatives might insist their version is still better.

The approximately 12.8-inch circular display also brings album artwork into that shared space. For a parent who remembers buying a particular record, its cover could be the beginning of a story you’ve never heard. For a partner, it might recall the album that accompanied your first road trip. The screen gives those visual associations room to register, rather than leaving them tucked away on a phone.

There’s dedicated audio hardware behind those moments, too. The R1 combines a 6.5-inch subwoofer with separate midrange drivers and tweeters in a five-driver, 2.1-channel system, developed in partnership with audio expert Jamo. That arrangement keeps the listening setup within one enclosure, without separate speaker cabinets to position around the room. That consolidated format has an obvious appeal for someone who prefers fewer objects around their favorite chair.

The first playlist could be part of the present, too, especially if it includes songs you’ve shared over the years. Bluetooth handles playback, while the MorningBlues app supports setup and the lyric experience. Once everything’s ready, you could spend Christmas afternoon working through those tracks together. There’s something pleasantly personal about explaining why you picked a song, even if the recipient immediately questions your taste.

After the guests leave, the R1 can accompany a quieter part of the holiday. A favorite album beside the reading chair offers a different evening from another round of television, while clock mode gives the display a purpose between listening sessions. Someone who treasures those slower hours at home will surely appreciate how the gift becomes part of a routine that continues well beyond the Christmas break.

Its warm ambient lighting, built-in audio, and wireless charging bring practical comforts to their evening routine without adding more bedside devices.

candidates.title: The hour hides inside an arrow on this revived Art Deco dial
candidates.full_text:
The HU-02 from Singapore maker Horologically Unique has no hour hand and no minute hand. A single Art Deco arrow turns around the dial with a window at its tip that shows the hour, and the arrow’s position against the minute track tells the minutes.

The display revives Robert Cart’s Chronoscope, built for pocket watches in the 1920s, and the brass version starts at $3,850.

Horologically Unique calls the display a wandering and jumping hour with a rotating minutes indicator, and the name describes exactly what happens on the dial. The arrow sweeps the full circle once an hour, and as it crosses from 59 to 60 the window at its tip jumps to the next hour.

The arrow itself carries an Art Deco guilloche, cut into both the cream Classic dial and the two-tone silver grain dial of the Silver Speciale.

Horologically Unique HU-02 Classic Naval brass case, mirror polished with a protective coating · Cream dial · Sand Calf strap Price: $3,850 Where to buy: Buy at Horologically Unique

The case measures 38.0mm across and 38.0mm lug to lug, so there’s no overhang past the strap line at either end, and the whole watch sits on the wrist as a simple round disc. Thickness runs 11.5mm with the domed sapphire crystal fitted and 10.1mm without the glass counted, and the crystal carries anti-reflective and anti-fingerprint coatings.

The strap attaches on an 18mm curved lug width and tapers from 18mm to 16mm at the buckle, with quick-release fittings on both versions.

The base movement is an ETA 2824-2 automatic, modified with a custom wandering hour module that Horologically Unique fits to drive the rotating arrow and the jumping window. The finishing is perlage and Cotes de Geneve, visible through the caseback, and the power reserve runs 32 hours. Water resistance is 3 ATM, which is splash territory rather than swimming depth.

The Classic pairs a mirror-polished naval brass case, protected by a coating, with a cream dial and a Sand Calf strap at $3,850. The Silver Speciale runs a mirror-polished 316L steel case with the silver grain dial and a Taupe Calf strap at $3,980. Both prices include shipping, though customs and taxes sit with the buyer, and the maker’s FAQ warns that US buyers may face significant tariffs on top.

Allocations stay open until the end of December 1, 2026, delivery is estimated for June to July 2027, and the maker states the run is limited by production and won’t be made again after this window. The trade is plain: you pay now and wait about seven months for a watch from a one-person project, and in exchange you get a display almost nobody else sells at this price, in a run that won’t repeat.

Horologically Unique HU-02 Silver Speciale 316L stainless steel case · Two-tone silver grain dial · Taupe Calf strap · 38.0mm case Price: $3,980 Where to buy: Buy at Horologically Unique

Buy the Classic at $3,850 if a brass case and the cream dial fit the collection you’re building, and take the Silver Speciale at $3,980 if you’d rather have the steel version. Skip both if you need a watch on your wrist this year, because nothing about this order arrives before next summer.

candidates.title: Four Toolheads. One Rail. Nothing Swaps. Meet the $649 Co Print Quadro 3D Printer
candidates.full_text:
Every craft that works in color figured this out long ago. A painter doesn’t rinse one brush between every color; there’s a brush for each one on the palette. Weavers load a separate shuttle for every thread. Pastry chefs fill a piping bag for every shade of frosting. Nobody scrubs one tool clean between colors, because the right one is already waiting. 3D printing took a while to catch up. Most multicolor printers still run every color through one nozzle, and newer four-in-one heads squeeze four colors through a single tip, so every material has to behave the same way. Co Print’s Quadro follows the craftsman’s rule instead: one tool per color. Four independent toolheads, each with its own filament, nozzle and temperature, share a single rail and take turns printing. It’s the oldest trick in the studio, finally built into a 3D printer.

If you’ve printed in multicolor on a single-nozzle machine, you already know about the poop. Every color change forces the printer to flush out the old filament, leaving a pile of rainbow waste that can outweigh the model itself. Toolchangers like the Snapmaker U1 avoid that flushing by picking up and parking whole heads, taking about five seconds per swap. The Quadro skips the pickup entirely, sliding the next head in as the last one leaves, in about one second. Add up to four materials in one print, a 300mm (11.8-inch) cube build volume and early pricing of $649, and this bed-slinger is aiming pretty high.

A $649 multi-material 3D printer with 1-second color changes, up to 90% less filament waste and a 300mm build cube, now live on Kickstarter.

Co Print calls the system IQEX, short for Independent Quad Extruder, and it extends the familiar dual-head IDEX layout to four. Each head gets its own stepper motor and belt, with four belts stacked one above another along the gantry. All four ride a shared 12mm linear rail, which means they physically can’t pass each other. Instead, idle heads tuck into docking stations at either end, clearing the bed for whichever head is working. That’s how every head reaches the full 300 × 300mm print area.

During a color change, the active head drives toward its dock while the incoming head moves into position. Co Print’s real-time footage shows a Tool 1 to Tool 2 handoff taking 1.00 seconds, with switches to Tool 3 and Tool 4 taking 1.40 and 1.57 seconds. That compares with roughly 60 seconds for a filament change on a single-nozzle printer, and Co Print says Quadro cuts filament waste by up to 90%. Nothing gets unclipped, grabbed, or reloaded during the handoff, avoiding the grippers and couplings used by toolchangers.

The parking spots are called QDock Stations, and each one holds up to three heads. As a head docks, its filament retracts slightly and its nozzle tip gets sealed to limit oozing and keep stray blobs off the print. Parked heads also cool to around 140°C to further reduce leakage. About 30 seconds before a head is needed, the printer starts heating it back to its target temperature. The aim is to have it ready to extrude when it leaves the dock.

Since each filament stays in its own nozzle, there’s no need to flush one color out before loading another. The Quadro does print a small prime tower, though, to establish nozzle pressure when a parked head starts extruding again. Zero Waste Mode moves that step into the model’s infill, eliminating the tower on compatible prints. In Co Print’s own four-color chameleon test, the Quadro finished in 9 hours 34 minutes with 34.16g of waste. The single-nozzle printer in the comparison needed just over a day and produced 180.7g of waste, while the toolchanger took 10 hours 5 minutes and produced 44.65g. That’s more than 14 hours faster than the single-nozzle machine, with about 80% less waste. In a larger scale test, the same four-color model left 1,079g of waste on a single-nozzle printer and just 135g on the Quadro.

Co Print chose a bed-slinger layout, where the build plate moves along the Y-axis, for its relative simplicity and ease of maintenance compared with CoreXY. The frame uses thick-section aluminum rather than thin bent sheet metal, and the load-bearing joints are metal-to-metal. Co Print says roughly 70% of the structure is metal. Even the bed carriage is a single piece of aluminum, designed to stay flat and parallel during high-speed printing.
